title: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)
paragraph: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) is a landmark public cancer genomics resource from the National Cancer Institute comprising multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics) for tens of thousands of tumors across 33 cancer types. Cao2022 uses TCGA pan-cancer (n=4,982 post-QC) to estimate tumor mRNA expression (TmS) across 15 cancer types. Dai2026 uses TCGA BRCA (n=83 TNBC) for chemotherapy-response stratification. Zatzman2022 applies hypertranscription analysis (RNAmp) to 7,494 TCGA tumors spanning 31 cancer types. Zhang2021 uses TCGA breast cancer for joint graphical network reconstruction across subtypes. Courau2025 references TCGA for TME archetype characterization alongside the UCSF Immunoprofiler cohort. Bentham2025 uses 14,501 cancer cases from the 100,000 Genomes Project rather than TCGA directly.

This is a high-quality batch. Content is factual, well-structured, non-promotional, and consistently
maps each paper to specific project hypotheses with appropriately hedged relevance framing.
Every spot-checked central claim (sample sizes, ORRs, IC50s, mechanism, cell lines, datasets) that
could be verified against a present PDF was faithful to the source — no hallucinations found. The
defects identified are almost all schema/cross-reference hygiene rather than fidelity problems.
Roughly **49 of 53 files (~92%) are clean**; the issues are concentrated in two broken `related:`
cross-references in one file, one malformed `source_refs` self-reference, and a low-severity schema
convention split. No BLOCKER-class factual errors.

paragraph: Scanned `doc/plans/` (16 plan documents, all dated 2026-05-01/02 covering Phases 3–7). All plan-driven work has either been retired (lap closed) or already mapped to the routing tasks in `tasks/active.md`. **No untracked implementation work detected** in the plan corpus.

title: NCI-60 Cancer Cell Line Panel
paragraph: The NCI-60 is a panel of 60 human cancer cell lines from nine tissue types maintained by the National Cancer Institute's Developmental Therapeutics Program, extensively profiled for drug sensitivity and molecular features. Ortmayr2019 uses 54 adherent cell lines from the NCI-60 panel with high-throughput metabolomics (FIA-TOFMS, >2000 metabolites), transcriptomics (54,875 probes), and proteomics to construct a genome-scale TR-activity to metabolite association map.

title: Truveta EHR (De-identified Longitudinal US Electronic Health Records)
paragraph: Truveta EHR is a de-identified longitudinal electronic health records dataset aggregated from more than 30 US health systems encompassing over 900 hospitals and more than 120 million patients. It covers structured clinical modalities including conditions, observations, lab results, medications, procedures, and demographics, with incident diagnoses coded using SNOMED CT, ICD-9-CM, and ICD-10-CM. The dataset is proprietary and not publicly accessible. Zeng2026 uses a matched case-control subset spanning 15 cancer types (500 cases + 500 controls per type) to evaluate TrajOnco, a multi-agent LLM framework for multi-cancer early detection from patient EHR trajectories.

title: Prostate NEPC serial subtype-transition inventory (Skerget analog layer)
paragraph: For a five-state transition matrix with row-stochastic constraints, each row contains four free parameters; a coarse rule-of-thumb for stable multinomial MLE is ~10 transitions per free parameter, i.e. **~40 outgoing transitions per origin state**, ~200 total. Stratifying by ≥2 lines of therapy multiplies that demand by the number of strata. Public tissue-serial-pair counts across Beltran 2016 + Aggarwal 2018 + SU2C-PCF re-biopsies sum to roughly low-tens to perhaps ~50 — adequate only for an **unstratified** 2- or 3-state collapse (e.g. {AR-active, AR-low/intermediate, NE-like}), not the full five-state matrix. **Rapid-autopsy multi-site sampling (UW-TAN, LuCaP donor cohort) is well-powered for state co-occurrence and stationary-state mixtures** — 52 patients × ~10 sites delivers >500 site-level subtype calls — but it does not identify transition direction or rate; treating sites as pseudo-serial conflates spatial heterogeneity with temporal change and assumes shared lineage at the metastatic level, which is at best partially supported (Kumar/Hong clonal-origin work). **Recommendation for t021**: budget for an unstratified 3-state (AR-active / AR-low-or-amphicrine / NE-like) trans

title: 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP)
paragraph: The 100,000 Genomes Project (Genomics England) is a UK national whole-genome sequencing initiative enrolling patients with rare diseases and cancer, providing WGS data linked to clinical records at unprecedented scale. Bentham2025 applies ImmuneLENS to 90,232 WGS samples from 100KGP, comprising 14,501 cancer cases across 33 distinct histologies plus 30,565 healthy germline samples and 13,870 matched blood samples, to characterize systemic immune dysregulation in aging and cancer.

title: TRACERx (TRAcking Cancer Evolution through therapy)
paragraph: TRACERx is a prospective multi-region sequencing study of lung cancer tracking tumor evolution from diagnosis through treatment and relapse; TRACERx 100 is the first 100-patient release. Cao2022 uses TRACERx (52 patients, 116 tumor samples, 94 regions from 30 patients with ≥2 regions) to examine the relationship between TmS and intra-tumor heterogeneity. Bentham2025 uses TRACERx 100 lung cancer samples with matched WES, RNA-seq Danaher scores, and blood count data from 441 participants to validate ImmuneLENS immune-fraction inference from WGS.

title: Many Labs 2
paragraph: Many Labs 2 is a large-scale multi-site replication project in psychology in which 28 classic and contemporary findings were tested across 125 samples from 36 countries/territories. Maier2022 uses the Many Labs 2 dataset as one of two empirical demonstrations for the RoBMA (Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis) method, illustrating how model-averaged publication-bias correction operates on a well-known multi-site replication dataset.

title: FinnGen (Finnish Biobank Genomics Initiative)
paragraph: FinnGen is a large Finnish population biobank initiative with genotyping and linked national health registry data. Participants are genotyped with Illumina arrays and imputed using a Finnish-specific whole-genome reference panel. Summary statistics for many disease endpoints are publicly available at https://www.finngen.fi/en/access_results. Carver2026 uses FinnGen (n ≈ 379,154 participants) as a replication cohort in a three-cohort germline GWAS meta-analysis for rare cancers, combining FinnGen summary statistics with PROFILE and MSK-IMPACT individual-level results. Long2023 references FinnGen as one of the cancer GWAS sources within the IEU Open GWAS project for outcome summary statistics in two-sample Mendelian randomisation.

title: Prostate NEPC mutation/selection-regime inventory (Persi analog layer)
paragraph: dNdScv's power scales with the count of nonsynonymous mutations per gene across the cohort. Prostate primary TMB at ~1 nsSNV/Mb over a ~30 Mb exome implies ~30 coding mutations per tumor; mCRPC at ~3-5 nsSNV/Mb implies ~90-150 coding mutations per tumor. Compared to post-treatment MM (Persi cohort), this is ~3-10x lower per-sample mutation count, and the prostate post-treatment cohort sizes are ~5-20x smaller (hundreds, not thousands). Detecting a treatment-vs-baseline shift in global dN/dS at alpha=0.05 with reasonable power (say 80%) on a moderate effect (e.g. dN/dS shift from ~1.0 to ~1.2-1.3, as seen in Persi) requires either (a) ~10^3-10^4 post-treatment exomes, or (b) restricting to mutation-rich subsets (MSI-H ~3% of mCRPC -> n=~12-30 across SU2C, too small) or to specific gene sets where prior knowledge sharply lowers the multiple-testing burden. Gene-level dNdScv is therefore borderline only for the ~10-30 most-mutated cancer driver genes in the pooled SU2C+Quigley cohort (~500 mCRPC), and **not feasible** for genome-wide treatment-stratified dN/dS at the resolution Persi achieves in MM. SOPRANO (immune-evasion-targeted dN/dS) and dndsv2 inherit the same per-mutation count

title: Does GCN-based drug synergy prediction trained on multi-disease auxiliary data
paragraph: [[Pourmousa2025]] showed that a GCN trained on PANC-1 combinations plus NCI-ALMANAC multi-disease auxiliary data achieved an 83% hit rate (vs. 40–53% for descriptor-based models) in prospective experimental validation. The question is whether this GCN architecture and transfer-learning approach generalizes to other cancer types, cell lines, or PDAC subtypes — i.e., whether auxiliary multi-disease pre-training is the driver of generalization rather than overfitting to PANC-1 compound activity patterns.

title: Published Meta-Analyses Corpus (Berenfeld2026)
paragraph: A corpus of 500 published meta-analyses assembled for empirical re-analysis of effect-measure collapsibility and target-population specification. Berenfeld2026 uses this corpus to demonstrate that conventional meta-analysis can yield misleading causal conclusions when effect-measure non-collapsibility (e.g., for odds ratios, risk ratios) or target-population ambiguity is ignored.

title: Does immunological age (circulating lymphocyte fraction) mediate the age-cancer-incidence
paragraph: [[Bentham2025]] (ImmuneLENS, 100,000 Genomes) shows circulating T-cell fraction is reduced in cancer patients, low circulating B-cell fraction precedes cancer diagnosis, and — strikingly — cancer patients' systemic immune profiles resemble those of healthy individuals ~40 years older. This raises whether **immunological age** (a systemic lymphocyte-fraction phenotype, measurable from WGS) is a mediator on the causal path from chronological age to cancer incidence, rather than a downstream consequence. This question sits at the boundary of `cancer/meta` and the health/meta aging frame.

title: Prostate NEPC convergence trio \u2014 feasibility / power check (go/no-go)
paragraph: **GO** for convergence-claim detection at moderate-or-larger effects (*dz* ≥ 0.6) on the Westbrook single-therapy primary; pooled cross-cohort at *dz* ≈ 0.5–0.6 is supplementary, contingent on mixed-effects pre-registration and site-as-covariate. Detecting small convergence effects (*dz* ≈ 0.3) is **not feasible** at any reachable n; the federation should not promise that resolution.

title: Non-MM convergence candidate: prostate adenocarcinoma to neuroendocrine prostate
paragraph:
Treatment-induced transition from prostate adenocarcinoma to **neuroendocrine
prostate cancer (NEPC)** remains the best first non-MM candidate after the
t022 scored comparison
([report:0029-t022-non-mm-convergence-anchor-scoring](../reports/0029-t022-non-mm-convergence-anchor-scoring.md)).
The structural pattern parallels MM closely while differing on lineage and
treatment class, which is exactly the contrast the federation needs to test
whether "convergence under selective therapy" is a portable model or an
MM-specific story.

title: MSK-IMPACT (Memorial Sloan Kettering Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable
paragraph: MSK-IMPACT is a clinically ascertained cancer sequencing cohort from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center using the IMPACT targeted panel (341–505 genes). Germline genotypes are imputed from tumor-panel sequencing using the STITCH framework. Carver2026 uses n = 54,945 patients from MSK-IMPACT as a second primary discovery cohort for germline GWAS across 20 rare cancer types, combined with PROFILE in a two-cohort meta-analysis (REMETA, inverse-variance weighted). Data are available under institutional data access agreements.

title: IEU Open GWAS Project
paragraph: The IEU Open GWAS project (MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit, University of Bristol) is a public repository of GWAS summary statistics spanning thousands of traits and diseases, accessible at https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/. It aggregates results from multiple large consortia including UK Biobank, BCAC, ILCCO, PRACTICA-L, MRC-IEU, OCAC, and Oncoarray. Long2023 uses IEU Open GWAS cancer outcome summary statistics (N up to 40,427 cases) for eight cancer types — breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, gastric, head and neck, endometrial, and ovarian — as the outcome source in a two-sample Mendelian randomisation analysis of gut microbiota causal effects on cancer risk.

paragraph:
The MM child question already lists three primary evidence inputs.
Each one is an independent claim with its own measurement layer, scale, and

title: BBQ (Bias Benchmark for QA)
paragraph: BBQ (Bias Benchmark for QA) is a question-answering benchmark designed to test social bias in language models across nine social categories, using ambiguous and disambiguated context scenarios. Si2025 uses BBQ alongside CrowS-Pairs and Winogender to evaluate implicit bias detection in large language models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3.1-70B) using Bayesian hypothesis testing with Bayes factors.

title: Phase 7 deep-read synthesis across the cancer federation
paragraph:
MM provides the clearest divergence-to-convergence case in the current federation.
multiple-myeloma:hypothesis:0004-attractor-convergence, multiple-myeloma:hypothesis:0005-positive-selection-mm-progression, Skerget 2024, Misund 2022, Persi 2025, and Ordonez 2020 collectively frame
a disease-local model: genetically and cytogenetically diverse plasma-cell
starting states can retain baseline structure while progression and relapse enrich
shared high-risk regulatory outputs. The convergent objects include PR-like
expression transition, E2F/G2M and metabolic pathway activation, chromatin
activation, and treatment-associated neutral dN/dS regime shifts. The central MM
paired-expression anchor is treatment-confounded: Misund 2022 cannot cleanly
separate natural progression from therapy-accelerated convergence because all
patients had intervening treatment exposure between samples. That makes the MM
case highly relevant to `question:0005-cross-cancer-resistance-mechanisms`, but
not a clean untreated-progression model.

title: PROFILE (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Clinically Sequenced Cohort)
paragraph: PROFILE is a clinically ascertained cancer cohort from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute comprising tumors from more than 62 cancer types sequenced with the OncoPanel targeted panel (275–447 genes). Germline genotypes are imputed from tumor-only panel sequencing using STITCH with the 1000 Genomes reference panel. Carver2026 uses n = 35,260 tumors from PROFILE as one of two primary discovery cohorts for germline GWAS across 20 rare cancer types, leveraging linked somatic, viral, and outcome data for mechanistic follow-up. Data are available under institutional data access agreements.

title: METABRIC (Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium)
paragraph: METABRIC is a large breast cancer genomics and transcriptomics study comprising microarray gene expression and genomic data from approximately 2,000 primary breast tumors with long-term clinical follow-up. Cao2022 uses METABRIC (n=1,546) for TmS-based survival analysis, finding that high TmS is associated with improved disease-free survival in TNBC patients treated with chemotherapy (n=118, DFS HR=0.5). Dai2026 applies TmS-based TME stratification to METABRIC (n=118 TNBC, European ancestry) as one of four validation cohorts for chemotherapy response prediction.

title: SCAN-B (Sweden Cancerome Analysis Network\u2014Breast)
paragraph: SCAN-B is a Swedish population-based breast cancer study with RNA-seq profiling and long-term clinical follow-up, representing a primarily European ancestry cohort. Dai2026 uses SCAN-B (n=144 TNBC, Swedish/European ancestry) as one of four validation cohorts for TmS-based TME stratification of chemotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer; SCAN-B also provides the DEG analysis replication set alongside TCGA.

title: MiBioGen (Microbiome and Genetics Consortium GWAS)
paragraph: MiBioGen is a large multi-ethnic gut microbiome GWAS consortium (Wang et al. 2022, *Microbiome*) characterising the genetic architecture of gut microbial composition. The dataset spans n = 18,340 participants across 24 cohorts using 16S rRNA sequencing for microbiota profiling (211 taxa across 5 taxonomic levels: 9 phyla, 16 classes, 20 orders, 35 families, 131 genera) combined with genome-wide genotyping. Summary statistics are publicly available at https://mibiogen.gcc.rug.nl/. Long2023 uses MiBioGen as the exposure GWAS source for genetic instruments in a two-sample Mendelian randomisation analysis of gut microbiota effects on eight cancer types.
